full_judgment: 37. But in Clause 8(b) of the policy and from the letter of repudiation dated 26-2-89 Exhibit 20, where the appellant has clearly repudiated the claim and also said that "we are closing the file as No Claim", we do not find any ambiguity in the letter of repudiation nor we find that the respondent had faced any ambiguity in understanding the meaning of this letter Exhibit 20 for initiating as action, which is clear from legal notice of the plaintiff as quoted above. In the book of Mac-Gillivray & Parkington on Insurance Law referred by Mr. Islam, in section 1175 at page 494 it is said that "the Rule is not, however, to be used to create ambiguity where none exists. One must not use the rule to create the ambiguity-one must find the ambiguity first. The basic presumption is that the words should receive their ordinary and natural meaning, and this is displaced only when there is a real ambiguity either appearing on the face of the policy or, possibly, revealed by extrinsic evidence of surrounding circumstances. If the meaning of the words is reasonably clear it must have full effect even though it operates harshly against the assured. It would not be in the interest of trade or the public generally to disregard the obvious meaning of words and to try to wring from them a hidden meaning in favour of the assured, and there is no other reason apart from ambiguity to strain the language of the policy in favour of the assured." So it is very clear that section 1173 cannot be used to create ambiguity against the company in favour of the assured when the language is very clear and there exists no ambiguity.
